questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: A pictograph shows books read by Mia. Each star stands for 5 books. Mia has 4 stars. How many books did Mia read?

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: In a pictograph, each smiley face stands for 2 students. Seven students chose cricket. How should cricket be shown?
questions.explanation: 7 is 3 twos and 1 left over. One left over is half a face, so 3 and a half faces.

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: A column graph counts koalas in a park. The side scale goes up in tens: 0, 10, 20, 30. The koala column ends halfway between 20 and 30. How many koalas are there?

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: Zoe will draw a column graph. Her numbers are 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100. Which scale on the side suits her best?
questions.explanation: All her numbers are in the 20 times table. Going up by 20s fits and the graph stays a good size.

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: The top temperatures in Perth over 7 days were 24, 25, 24, 26, 25, 24 and 25 degrees. What can we say about this data?
choices: The temperatures were very close together
The temperatures were all the same
The temperatures went up by 10 degrees
questions.explanation: All the numbers are between 24 and 26. They hardly vary.

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: A pictograph uses one symbol for 10 people. Why is it hard to show exactly 47 people?
choices: Part of a symbol is hard to read exactly
47 is too big for a pictograph
Symbols cannot be used for people
questions.explanation: 47 is 4 whole symbols and 7 out of 10 of another. It is hard to draw and read that part exactly.

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: Liam scored these goals in 7 games: 2, 3, 2, 4, 2, 3, 9. One score is very different from the others. What is that score?
questions.explanation: Most scores are from 2 to 4. The 9 is far away from them.

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: A bag has 9 red marbles and 1 blue marble. You pick one without looking. Which colour is most likely?
questions.explanation: There are more red marbles than blue, so red is most likely.

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: Which pair of events is independent, so the first does not change the chances of the second?
choices: Take a card from a pack and keep it, then take another card
Roll a die, then roll it again
Take a red sock from a drawer and keep it, then take another sock
Take a raffle ticket from a drum and keep it, then take another
questions.explanation: Rolling a die once does not change the next roll. In the other pairs, an item is taken away, so the chances change.

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: It is certain that Sydney will be in summer in January.
questions.explanation: In Australia, summer is December to February. January is always in summer.

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: Ravi rolls a normal die with faces 1 to 6. Which event is impossible?
questions.explanation: The die only has the numbers 1 to 6, so a 7 can never happen.

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: Ella flipped a coin 20 times. She got 12 heads and 8 tails. How many more heads than tails did she get?

questions.subject: maths
questions.prompt: Two groups each spin the same spinner 20 times. Group A gets red 8 times. Group B gets red 11 times. Why are the results different?
choices: Chance results can be different each time
questions.explanation: Chance experiments give different results each time, even when done the same way.
